guide.title: What happens when your callback is down
guide.subtitle: Retries, ordering and the one state that never calls back
guide.excerpt: Terminal outcomes are pushed to a URL you control, with a small bounded retry. Your handler has to tolerate a repeat, and it should not expect a call for every message.

p: Any non-2xx response or a timeout triggers a retry after roughly one second, then five, then fifteen. Three attempts, then the platform gives up and records the callback as failed. Bounded retries are the honest shape: an endpoint that is down for an hour is not going to be fixed by a queue that keeps hammering it.
The practical consequence is that a callback you miss during a deploy is missed permanently. Reconcile from the message log rather than expecting a later delivery.

sections.h: Assume you may see it twice
p: A retry can arrive after a response that was slow rather than lost, so duplicates are possible. De-duplicate on the message ID on your side. The platform sends the request with a callback token header, which your handler should verify before trusting the payload.

sections.h: Not every message produces a callback
list: Only terminal outcomes are pushed. A message that is still in flight is not reported by callback.
A suppressed message never reaches a provider, so it has no delivery outcome to report — its final state is decided at acceptance time.
Callback delivery is asynchronous: a message can be delivered and its callback still in flight, so treat "no callback yet" as unknown rather than as failure.
sections.scope: Delivery receipt collection and forwarding are implemented for the SMS channel.
